 Judgment:

1. The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (PFA Act), alleging that the accused persons have violated the provisions of the PFA Act and Rules.
The accused no.1 is stated to be the vendor-cum-proprietor of M/s. National General Store from where the food article, that is, 'Culinary Sauce' was lifted for sampling.

Accused no.3 is stated to be In Re vs A-1) Harish Kumar Ahuja on 19 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/164683348/
1
the Company, of which accused no.2 was the Nominee, that had supplied the food article to accused no.1.

Accused no.5 is stated to be the Manufacturing Firm, of which accused no.4 is the Nominee,
that had supplied the food article to accused no.3.
2.

As per the complaint, on 29.09.2008, the food officials consisting of Food Inspectors (FI)
Chander Bhan Boora and Field Assistant (FA) J. S. Bisht under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. Pradeep Baijal reached along with their staff at the premises of M/s.
National General Store (Proprietorship concern of accused no.1), at 877, Multani Building, Qutub Road, Delhi-06, where the accused no.1 was found conducting the business of various food articles which were lying stored for sale for human consumption.

The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of 'Culinary Sauce' from the vendor as lying in sealed plastic containers of 300 grams each bearing identical label declaration, to which he agreed.
A sample of 3 such sealed containers of 300 grams each was then lifted and divided in three parts as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules.

Each sample was separately packed,
fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the notice as per Form-VI, panchnama etc.
The price of sample was paid to the vendor.
Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.

Vide report dated 31.10.2008, the PA found the sample to be misbranded on the ground that it was giving misleading information regarding nature of article which was labelled as Mayonnaise (a proprietary item) as well as 'Culinary Sauce' (which was a standardized item and a fruit product).
Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by FI.
Various letters were issued by the FI to ascertain the details of the distributor and supplier.
It was found that the accused no.1 had purchased the food article from accused no.3 Company that had in turn procured the same from accused no.5 partnership firm.
Accused no.2 and accused no.4 were the Nominees of accused no.3 and accused no.5 respectively.
After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.
The complaint was then filed in the court on 25.02.2010 against all the accused persons alleging violation of section 2(ix)(g) and (k) of PFA Act, as punishable section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused persons were summoned vide order dated 25.02.2010.

The accused persons appeared and filed an application under section 13(2) of PFA Act thereby exercising the right to get the second counterpart of the sample to be analysed from Central Food Laboratory (CFL).
The application was allowed and a counterpart was sent for analysis to CFL.

The CFL examined the sample and its Director gave Certificate dated 01.04.2010, opining the sample to be not conforming to the standards of 'Culinary Paste / Sauce' as per PFA Rules due to presence of acidity less than the prescribed minimum limit.

4. Based on the CFL report, notice of accusation under section 251 CrPC was framed against all the accused persons on 09.06.2010 for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1)(a)
PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of PFA Act, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.

In Re vs A-1) Harish Kumar Ahuja on 19 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/164683348/
2 5.

Subsequently, an application under section 19(2) of PFA Act was filed which was dispose of vide order dated 04.07.2014 and the benefit of warranty was granted to the accused no.1, 2 and 3 and they were acquitted of the charges.
Subsequent trial was faced by accused no.4 and 5 and this judgement is with respect to these accused persons only.
6. At the trial, the prosecution examined two witnesses in support of its case.
PW-1 FI C. B. Boora and PW-2 Sh. Pradeep Baijal were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings along with FI J. S. Bisht.

Both these witnesses deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 29.09.2008 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity, expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of three sealed plastic containers of 300 gram each of 'Culinary Sauce', dividing it in three parts by treating one sealed container as one counterpart, fastening, sealing, marking the sample counterparts, and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses.

They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex. PW-1/A, notice Ex. PW-1/B, panchnama Ex. PW-1/C,
notice under section 14A Ex. PW-1/D, raid report Ex. PW-1/E, PA Receipt Ex. PW-1/F and LHA receipt Ex. PW-1/G. PA report Ex. PW-1/H was received and investigation was conducted by PW-1.
He sent various letters to various departments and the accused persons and sought their replies during the investigation.
After completion of investigation, sanction Ex. PW-1/L was taken from the Director PFA and the complaint Ex. PW-1/M was filed in the court by PW-1.
A copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex. PW-1/N was sent to the accused persons through post.

These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence Counsel for accused no.4 and 5 wherein they denied that the accused persons had been falsely implicated or that a false complaint was filed.
7. Statement of the accused no.4 (also representing accused no.5) under section 313 CrPC was recorded on 17.10.2016 wherein he denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.
He expressed ignorance about the sample proceedings as he was not present at the spot, though he denied the PA and CFL reports claiming that the product was as per standards.
He did not lead any evidence in defence.

8. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused no.4 and 5 beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that the accused persons have not been able to rebut the findings in the CFL report dated 01.04.2010 which as per section 13(3) of PFA Act is final and conclusive.
It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony.

It is a matter of record that vide statement dated 04.07.2014, accused no.4 and 5 admitted that the product in question as lifted from accused no.1 and as supplied to him by accused no .3, belonged to them.

9. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly and that there are various contradictions and missing links in the testimony of witnesses.

Ld. Counsel has strongly contended that there is variation in the reports as given by PA and CFL, which leads to conclusion that the two samples were not representative and therefore,
conviction cannot be based solely on the basis of the CFL report.

In Re vs A-1) Harish Kumar Ahuja on 19 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/164683348/
3 10.
I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant and Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused and have carefully perused the material available on record.
11. It is to be understood that the notice framed against the accused is for violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of the PFA Act on the basis of CFL report.

Under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature,
substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature, substance or quality which it purported or represented to be.
Section 2(ia)(m) on the other hand applies when the quality or purity of an article falls below the prescribed standards which does not render the article injurious to health.

At the same time, it is pertinent to note that as per the PA report, the food article was only misbranded and there was no opinion to the effect that the product was adulterated or was not conforming to the prescribed standards.
However, as per the CFL report, there was no opinion that the product was misbranded and the opinion given is to the effect that the product was not conforming to the standards.
12. In the case at hand, the product is stated to be Culinary Sauce and it was tested by the CFL on the basis of standards prescribed for Culinary Sauce.

It is also an admitted position that the label on the product mentioned the words "Culinary Sauce" as well as "Mayonnaise".
13.
It is to be noted that as per the PFA Rules, certain standards have been prescribed with respect to several food articles in Appendix-B.
Such food articles are standardized food articles which are required to conform to the prescribed standards.
The other food articles which are not so standardized under the PFA Rules, would be called as proprietary food article as defined in Rule 37A of PFA Rules.

14. As per the PFA Rules, Culinary Sauce fell in the category of "Culinary Pastes / Fruits and Vegetable Sauces other than Tomato Sauce and Soya Sauce" under Item No. A.16.28(3) of Appendix-B of PFA Rules, under the larger head A.16 as "Fruit Products".
Therefore, Culinary Sauce is a standardized food article.
However, Mayonnaise as a food product has not been standardized as no separate standards have been prescribed for any such product called Mayonnaise.
There is nothing under the PFA Rule to ascertain what product would be called Mayonnaise and what would be its ingredients.
There is nothing to show that the product in question was not Mayonnaise or Culinary Sauce or both.
15. The PA report is also doubtful as to if the product in question was a milk product or a fruit product.
As per PA report Ex. PW-1/H, it is mentioned that the sample was found to be a "milk product".
But there is nothing to show as to on what basis the PA opined the product to be a milk product when there is nothing to show that there was any milk fat / content therein.
Even the quality characteristics on which the sample was tested nowhere shows presence of any such milk content.
The ingredients on the label of the food product mentions milk solids as well as lime juice along with vegetable oil, water, sugar, salt and other preservatives, agents and acids.
Therefore, it could fall in both the categories of milk product as well as fruit product.
Since no standards of Mayonnaise have been prescribed, there can be no question of violation of any such standard.

In Re vs A-1) Harish Kumar Ahuja on 19 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/164683348/
4 16.
The product in question was considered as Culinary Sauce by the CFL on the basis of label declaration.
As per section 13(3) of the PFA Act, the certificate issued by the Director of CFL shall supersede the report of the PA.
As per proviso to section 13(5) of the Act, such certificate shall be final and conclusive evidence for the facts stated therein.
Thus, as far as the findings of the CFL are concerned, the same are final and conclusive and no evidence can be given to disprove the same.

17. In Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf [AIR 1999 SC 738], it has been authoritatively laid down that the legal impact of a certificate of the Director of CFL is three fold: (a)
it annuls or replaces the report of the PA, (b) it gains finality regarding the quality and standard of the food article involved in the case and (c) it becomes irrefutable so far as the facts stated therein are concerned.
18.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In Subhash Chander v. State, Delhi Administration [1983(4) DRJ 100], it was observed by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi that "It has repeatedly been held by the supreme court that the certificate of the Director supersedes the report of the public analyst and is to be treated as conclusive evidence of its contents.

entities.text: Subhash Chander v. State, Delhi Administration [1983(4) DRJ 100]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Director is a greater expert and therefore the statute says that his certificate shall be accepted by the court as conclusive evidence.
For all purposes the report of the public analyst is replaced by the certificate of the Director....
Superseded is a strong word.
It means obliterate, set aside, annul, replace, make void, inefficacious or useless, repeal.
The Director's certificate supersedes the report given by the public analyst.
Once superseded it does not survive for any purpose.
It will be anomalous to hold that for some purpose it survives and for other purposes it is superseded."
19. Since the report of CFL is final and conclusive and the same supersedes the report of PA, only this report has to be considered and the report of PA has to be ignored.

However, the defence strongly relies upon the judgement titled as Kanshi Nath v. State [2005(2) FAC 219], informing that the said ruling has been constantly followed by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in State v. Ramesh Chand [2010 (2) JCC 1250], Food Inspector v.
Parvinder Malik [2014(2) FAC 306], State v. Vinod Kumar Gupta [2010(2) JCC 957], State v.
Virender Kohli [2014(2) FAC 223], State v. Kamal Aggarwal [2014(2) FAC 183], State v. Vidya Gupta [2014(1) FAC 291], State v. Dinesh Goswami [2014(1) FAC 302], State v. Mahabir [2014(1) FAC 286], and State v. Santosh Sharma [2014(1) FAC 296].

sentences.text: It is submitted that comparison of the two reports would show that there are substantive variations which would show that the sample was not representative.

20. The Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Kashi Nath's case (supra), was dealing with a situation where there were certain variations in the reports of PA and CFL while analysing a sample of 'dhania powder'.

Hon'ble Court considered the ratio in MCD v. Bishan Sarup [ILR 1970 (1) Delhi 518] and held that it would still be open for the accused to establish that the sample tested was not a representative one, and if the variation in the two reports is substantial enough, then the PA report can certainly be looked into to establish this variation.
In Re vs A-1) Harish Kumar Ahuja on 19 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/164683348/
5 21.

sentences.text: Therefore, it can be safely said that though the CFL report is final and conclusive as to the results therein, yet it can still be looked into to ascertain if the samples were representative or not.

If the accused is able to show that the samples were not representative or otherwise that the food article might have undergone a change by the time it reached CFL which was beyond his control, he would get benefit on that count.
22. Visibly, the CFL never opined the sample to be misbranded.
There is no opinion that the label declaration was misleading in any manner.
The sample was treated as Culinary Sauce as per Item No. A.16.28(3).
Even if the food article is treated as Culinary Sauce, the differences between the two reports would show substantive variations in the two.
The PA did not test the presence of acidity at all, in the absence of which the court cannot assume that the acidity was less then the minimum prescribed limit and if so, to what extent.
As far as PA report is concerned, the CFL report negated the report of PA on the sole incriminating parameter on the basis of which the prosecution was launched.
No misbranding was found by the CFL.

The only ground on which the CFL failed the sample was the presence of acidity as acetic acid to be 0.26% which was less then the prescribed minimum limit of 1.0%.
23.
Though the CFL report is final and conclusive as to the results therein, yet it can still be looked into to ascertain if the samples were representative or not.

If the accused is able to show that the samples were not representative or otherwise that the food article might have undergone a change by the time it reached CFL which was beyond his control, he would get benefit on that count.

24. As far as acidity content is concerned, it is important to understand that fruit and milk products are having very less shelf life and are prone to natural changes with the passage of time, particularly after expiry of their best before date.

As per the label declarations reproduced by the FI on Form VI,
Ex. PW- 1/D, the product was manufactured on 30.08.2008 and its best before date was four months from the date of manufacture that comes out to be 30.12.2008.
Therefore, the product might not be of the prescribed standards after expiry of the best before date.

Where the quality or purity of an article has fallen below the prescribed standards solely due to natural causes and beyond the control of human agency, then such article shall may not be considered adulterated.
25. The CFL had examined the sample from 23.03.2010 to 01.04.2010.
Thus, it was so analyzed after about 1 year and 6 months when it was lifted from the possession of the accused no.1.
The nature of such food article is such that some changes are bound to happen if sample is kept for a long period at room temperature.
The effect of air, moisture, internal heat and external environment etc. cannot be ignored on such article.
Such changes would be natural changes beyond human control.
26. Changes in acidity content would be covered under such changes.
During the long intervening period of 16 months, the possibility of such natural changes cannot be ruled out.
There is no explanation why the complaint itself was filed after 18 months of lifting the sample which would have in any case rendered the food article unfit for correct analysis.

The burden would be on prosecution to rule out possibility of such natural changes before the accused can be convicted,
particularly in view of such substantive variations in the two reports and the fact that no such In Re vs A-1) Harish Kumar Ahuja on 19 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/164683348/
6 irregularity was detected by the PA.
The only conclusion would be that the sample underwent a natural change during the intervening period which was beyond human control.
For this, the accused persons would get benefit of doubt.
27. Therefore, the matter would not be covered under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act.

There is no evidence to show that any particular nature, quality or substance of Culinary Sauce or Mayonnaise was demanded by the FI which was not supplied to him to his prejudice, or that it was not of nature,
quality or substance represented or purported to be, so as to bring the case within section 2(ia)(a) of the PFA Act.
If the product was Mayonnaise, no offence under section 2(ia)(a) or (m) would be made out as no standards had been prescribed for this article.

If the product was Culinary Sauce,
considering the time gap, natural variations and variations in two reports, the accused no.4 and 5 are entitled to be given benefit of doubt.

The evidence on record is not sufficient to conclude that the sample in question was 'adulterated' within the meaning of section 2(ia) of PFA Act and thus, no case would be made out against the accused no.4 and 5 for commission of offences punishable under section 7/16 of the PFA Act.
28.
Having said so, the accused no.4 and 5 are acquitted of the charges.

However, bail bond of accused no.4 shall remain in force for the next six months in terms of section 437-A CrPC.
29.
File be consigned to record room.
